# Reductive leaching of cathodic active materials from lithium ion battery wastes

Churl Kyoung Leea,\*, Kang-In Rheeb

Received 24 August 2001; received in revised form 12 March 2002; accepted 9 September 2002

## ABSTRACT

Reductive leaching of LiCoO2 from spent lithium ion battery was investigated in terms of reaction variables. The leaching efficiency of LiCoO2 increased with increasing temperature, and concentration of HNO3, but with decreasing solid/liquid (S/L) ratio. Li and Co from LiCoO were leached over 95% with the addition of 1.7 vol Ω^0 / ΩH2 O2 as a reducing agent. This is due to the reduction of Co ^3+ to Co ^2+ which can be readily dissolved. The dissolution rates of Co and Li were inversely proportional to their respective concentrations in the solution. Apparent activation energies of 12.5 and 11.4 kcal/mol were obtained for Co and Li, respectively. This indicates that the dissolution of LiCoO2 is controlled by surface chemical reaction. D 2003 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Lithium ion battery; Cathodic active materials; Reductive leaching; H2O2

## 1. Introduction

Recycling of lithium batteries has become important because, due to their characteristics of lightness and good performance (Lundblad and Bergman, 1997; Plichta and Salomon, 1987), these batteries are increasingly substituting for other batteries. In 2000, the worldwide production of lithium ion secondary batteries (LIBs) reached about 500 millions cells of which Korea has a 10% market share. From this consumption, LIB waste is annually estimated at 200 to 500 MT, with a metal content of 5 to 15 wt.% Co and 2 to 7 wt.% Li.

Spent lithium primary batteries cannot be disposed of unless the contained metallic lithium is properly removed, due to its explosive nature. Also, lithium cobalt oxide is adopted as cathodic active material; therefore, valuable metals such as cobalt and lithium have to be recycled (Sabin, 1997; Shackle and Calif, 1994; Suita, 1990; William et al., 1982; Zhang et al., 1998). Thus, there are two problems to be solved; disposal of harmful waste and prevention of explosion during recycling of LIB waste. Metallic lithium in the used LIBs can be formed on graphite anode by overcharging and abnormal deposition. Vigorous oxidation of metallic lithium with moisture can be dangerous during the mechanical treatment of spent LIBs. For successful recovery of cobalt and lithium from spent LIBs, safety in mechanical treatment, and waste minimization are considered to be the most important.

In this study, acid leaching has been applied to recover cobalt and lithium from cathodic active material of spent LIB. The cathodic active material was separated by physical processes involving thermal treatment, shredding, and vibrating screening as shown in Fig. 1 (Lee and Rhee, 2002). Thermal pretreatment was necessary for the separation of cell units from the battery package. However, it caused thermal hardening of the plastic casing, and partial oxidation of metallic lithium. Thus, the batteries were shredded for the liberation of electrode materials; a shredder was designed considering the selectivity of active materials as well as the reduction of cost and impurities (Lee and Rhee, 2000).

Reductive leaching of the cathodic active material with H2O2 addition in a nitric acid solution was employed for a better dissolution of cobalt and lithium. Effects of temperature, HNO3 concentration, solid/liquid (S/L) ratio, and H2O2 concentration were investigated. The kinetics of the reductive leaching was also studied.

## 2. Experimental procedures

A LIB consists of a plastic casing and several cell units. Each cell unit has a cathode, an anode, an organic separator, an organic electrolyte, and a Nicoated steel casing. In the cathode, LiCoO2 active materials, carbon-conducting additives, and a binder are pasted on aluminum foil. The anode is fabricated by the same process with graphite active materials, carbon-conducting additives, and a binder pasted on copper foil. Table 1 shows a typical chemical composition of the LIB.

Cathodic active material from lithium ion secondary battery was separated by a series of thermal treatment, high-speed shredding, calcination steps (Lee and Rhee, 2002). First, LIB samples were thermally treated in a muffle furnace at 150 ^∘C for 1 h. Then, the samples were disassembled with a highspeed shredder. Separated segments were simultaneously classified into the range 1–10 mm in size. Second, thermal treatment was performed in a furnace, and electrode materials were separated from the current collectors by vibrating screening. Next, cathodic active material, LiCoO2 was obtained by burning carbon and binder off in the temperature range 700– 900 ^∘C for 1 h. Fig. 2 shows XRD patterns of calcined cathodic active material at temperature of 700– 900 ^∘C.. The diffractogram indicates that the carbon and binder were burnt off by calcining above 800 ^∘C.. The cathodic active material was ground in a ball mill and dried in an oven at 60 ^∘C for 48 h. The mean particle size was about 15 Am, as shown in Fig. 3 (Lee and Rhee, 2002).

[TABLE:TABLE_Reductive Leaching of Cathodic Active Materials from Lithium Ion Battery Wastes_0001]

Leaching of LiCoO2 in nitric acid solution was tested in a reactor (Fig. 4), which was placed in a water bath to control the reaction temperature within ± 0.5 ^∘C. To obtain the optimum conditions of LiCoO2 leaching, leaching experiments were tested at various conditions, i.e. changing HNO3 concentration, S/L ratio, temperature, and H2O2 concentration. To increase leaching efficiency, reductive leaching was carried out in the presence of a reducing agent such as H2O2

The concentration of various metallic ions was measured using an atomic absorption spectrometer (Perkin-Elmer M3100) and inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer (JY-38). The solid phases in the cathodic active material were identified using an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku, Cu-Ka).

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Reductive leaching

Fig. 5 shows the leaching behavior of cathodic active materials in 1 M nitric acid solution when other conditions were fixed at 20 g/L S/L ratio and 75 ^∘C. In the absence of a reducing agent, the leaching efficiencies of the cobalt and lithium levelled off within 30 min with low extractions of 40% Co and 75% Li. To increase the leaching efficiency, 0.8 vol.% hydrogen peroxide was added as a reducing agent (Zhang et al., 1998). The extractions of both metals were improved to about 85% by the reductive leaching as shown in the figure. It seems that Co ^2 ^+ (cobaltous) is more readily dissolved than Co ^3+ (cobaltic).

To obtain the optimum conditions for the reductive leaching of LiCoO2, several sets of leaching experiments were made under different conditions, i.e. various HNO3 concentrations, S/L ratio, temperature, and H2O2 amount added. Fig. 6 shows the effect of HNO3 concentration on the leaching of LiCoO2 at 20 g/L S/L ratio, 75 ^∘ ^,, 0.8 vol.% H2O2,, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li increased with increasing HNO3 concentration. More than 80% of Co and Li was extracted within 30 min above 1 M HNO3

The leaching behavior with different S/L ratios is presented in Fig. 7 at a fixed condition of 1 M HNO3, 75 ^∘C, 0.8 vol.% H2O2, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li decreased with increasing S/L ratio. Extractions of 90% of Co and Li were achieved within 30 min when S/L ratio was lower than 20 g/L for H2O2 addition of 0.8 vol.%.

Fig. 8 shows the effect of temperature on the leaching at 10 g/L S/L ratio, 1 M HNO3, 1.7 vol.% H2O2, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li increased with increasing temperature. The extent of Co extraction was close to 99% at 75 ^∘C,, 75% at 50 ^∘C and 30% at 25 ^∘C, respectively, and that of Li was similar to Co extraction.

Fig. 9 shows the effect of H2O2 concentration on the leaching at 20 g/L S/L ratio, 1 M HNO3, 75 ^, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li increased with increasing H2O2 addition. The amount of 1.7 vol.% H2O2 was sufficient for the complete dissolution of Co and Li.

## 3.2. Kinetic considerations

Assuming that leaching of Co and Li has no interdependence and the dissolution rate is inversely proportional to their respective ionic concentrations (CCo and CLi), the square of Ci has a linear relationship with respect to reaction time as described by the following equation,

Ci ^2 = k t (Eq. 1)

where Ci represents the concentration of species i in the leaching solution(mol cm ^-3), k is the apparent rate constant (mol ^2 cm ^-6 s ^-1), and t is time (s). Fig. 10 is the plot of square of C vs. time, which is drawn from the effect of temperature (Fig. 8). From the linearity observed as shown in the case of Co (Fig. 10 (a)) and Li (Fig. 10(b)), the assumptions could be confirmed. Therefore, the dissolution rate of Co and Li was inversely proportional to their respective ionic concentrations. The apparent activation energy of Co and Li was calculated from the Arrhenius plot (Fig. 11) to be 12.5 and 11.4 kcal/mol, respectively. Therefore, the dissolution of LiCoO2 seems to be controlled by surface chemical reaction (Han and Lawson, 1980).

## 4. Conclusions

An investigation of leaching of LiCoO2 by the use of nitric acid led to the following conclusions.

1. By reductive leaching with the addition of hydrogen peroxide as a reducing agent, the leaching efficiency increased by 45% for Co and 10% for Li compared with that in only nitric acid leaching. This behavior seems to be due to the reduction of Co^3 + to Co2 +, which is readily dissolved. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li increased with increasing HNO3 concentration, temperature, and hydrogen peroxide concentration and with decreasing S/L ratio. An effective condition for the leaching would be 1 M HNO3, 10 to 20 g/L initial S/L ratio, 75 ^∘C temperature, and 1.7 vol.% H2O2 addition.

2. From the kinetic study, the dissolution rates of Co and Li were found to be inversely proportional to their respective ionic concentrations. The apparent activation energy was obtained as 12.5 and 11.4 kcal/mol for Co and Li, respectively. This indicates that the dissolution of LiCoO2 is controlled by surface chemical reaction.

## TABLE_ROLE_GATE_PROMPT
You are a table role gate for WEEE knowledge graph extraction.

Goal: decide the table-level extraction boundary before Semantic IR generation.

Allowed decisions:
- extract: the table reports target composition, a target-bearing treatment outcome, or current-study quantitative physical characterization of a WEEE/product/sample (for example total mass, component count, component mass, or component mass fraction). The outcome may be in a solid, liquid, or gas phase and does not require an isolated final product.
- context_extract: the table reports only inputs, setup, parameters, identifier mappings, reagents, media, or operating conditions, without target composition, treatment outcome, or quantitative product/component characterization.
- skip: the table reports neither current-study target composition nor a target-bearing treatment outcome, for example economics, literature summaries, unrelated background, or method validation alone.

Boundary notes:
- Follow the causal chain from source object through transformation to measured object. A post-treatment concentration, fraction, yield, or recovery measurement is an extractable result when it quantifies movement or presence of the target material caused by the treatment.
- Physical phase alone never determines the decision. A process medium used only as an input is context; the same medium measured after treatment as evidence of target transfer or recovery is a result.
- A table that measures process-internal agents or biological/chemical mechanism variables (for example culture metabolites, biomass, catalyst activity, or their concentrations) is out of scope unless it reports the movement, recovery, or transformation of a WEEE constituent. Use `skip`, not `extract`, for such a table.
- A table that reports economic value shares, prices, costs, or price-weighted distributions of target constituents is `skip`, even if the constituent names are target metals. Economic value share is not target composition; it is a monetary quantity derived from price and mass fraction.
- Words such as "obtained by", "dismantled", or "treated" do not make target composition context-only.
- Brand/model/sample identifiers are contextual fields, but their presence does not make measured mass, count, or component-weight columns context-only. Preserve the identifiers as the measured product identity and extract those quantitative observations.

Structured decision steps:
1. Identify `source_object`, `transformation`, `measured_object`, and `measured_quantity` from caption and reference text.
2. Classify `evidence_role` as target_composition, treatment_outcome, process_input, setup_context, or out_of_scope.
3. Use section, headers, and row preview only when caption and references leave a slot unresolved.
4. If evidence remains insufficient, lower confidence and state the unresolved slot; do not choose skip merely because the measured object is an intermediate phase.
5. If `structural_row_runs` is present, assign each run a semantic role and return the complete ranges that may emit final facts in `extract_row_ranges`. The ranges are 1-based and inclusive.

Return only valid JSON:

    "decision": "extract | context_extract | skip",
    "table_role": "target_composition | recovery_result | process_output | process_parameter | sample_metadata | economic_value | literature_summary | analytical_method | non_target_context | ambiguous",

    ],

  }
}

Keep all explanation in a short `rationale`.

Entity meanings:
- Product: complete WEEE item or product family, e.g. mobile phone, smartphone, laptop.
- Component: physical part/subassembly of a product, e.g. PCB, WPCB, waste printed circuit board, casing, battery.
- Material: a WEEE constituent, recovery target, recovered product, or WEEE-relevant transformation product, e.g. Cu, Ag, Au, LiCoO2. Do not create Material endpoints for experimental inputs or process-internal measurements (reagents, solvents, lixiviants, culture media, microbes, metabolites, catalysts, or their concentrations) unless the article explicitly frames that item itself as a recovered WEEE material.
- Process: treatment/recycling/separation/analysis step, e.g. leaching, pyrolysis, dismantling.
- Observation: a measured physical property of the source entity itself, e.g. total weight, particle size, moisture content.

- CONTAINS: container (Product/Component/Material) -> constituent (Component/Material), including composition, content, and part proportions measured after a process. ## 3. Results and discussion
## 3.1. Reductive leaching
Fig. 5 shows the leaching behavior of cathodic active materials in 1 M nitric acid solution when other conditions were fixed at 20 g/L S/L ratio and 75 ^∘C. In the absence of a reducing agent, the leaching efficiencies of the cobalt and lithium levelled off within 30 min with low extractions of 40% Co and 75% Li. To increase the leaching efficiency, 0.8 vol.% hydrogen peroxide was added as a reducing agent (Zhang et al., 1998). The extractions of both metals were improved to about 85% by the reductive leaching as shown in the figure. It seems that Co ^2 ^+ (cobaltous) is more readily dissolved than Co ^3+ (cobaltic).
To obtain the optimum conditions for the reductive leaching of LiCoO2, several sets of leaching experiments were made under different conditions, i.e. various HNO3 concentrations, S/L ratio, temperature, and H2O2 amount added. Fig. 6 shows the effect of HNO3 concentration on the leaching of LiCoO2 at 20 g/L S/L ratio, 75 ^∘ ^,, 0.8 vol.% H2O2,, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li increased with increasing HNO3 concentration. More than 80% of Co and Li was extracted within 30 min above 1 M HNO3
The leaching behavior with different S/L ratios is presented in Fig. 7 at a fixed condition of 1 M HNO3, 75 ^∘C, 0.8 vol.% H2O2, and 30 min. The leaching efficiency of Co and Li decreased with increasing S/L ratio. text_chunk.text:
## 3.2. Kinetic considerations
Assuming that leaching of Co and Li has no interdependence and the dissolution rate is inversely proportional to their respective ionic concentrations (CCo and CLi), the square of Ci has a linear relationship with respect to reaction time as described by the following equation, where Ci represents the concentration of species i in the leaching solution(mol cm ^-3), k is the apparent rate constant (mol ^2 cm ^-6 s ^-1), and t is time (s). Fig. 10 is the plot of square of C vs. time, which is drawn from the effect of temperature (Fig. 8). From the linearity observed as shown in the case of Co (Fig. 10 (a)) and Li (Fig. 10(b)), the assumptions could be confirmed. Therefore, the dissolution rate of Co and Li was inversely proportional to their respective ionic concentrations. The apparent activation energy of Co and Li was calculated from the Arrhenius plot (Fig. 11) to be 12.5 and 11.4 kcal/mol, respectively. Therefore, the dissolution of LiCoO2 seems to be controlled by surface chemical reaction (Han and Lawson, 1980).
